pages.text: Gold is native, the metal itself, alloyed with a tenth or so of silver. It forms in quartz veins, the lode, where hot water dropped it with stibnite and a little galena, and as the veins weather it washes down into river and beach sand, where its weight keeps it: the placers of the Klondike and of California in 1849.
pages.title: Gold

pages.text: Vanilla gold ore is native gold too, and mines as raw native gold.

Panning is a fan's wash: raw native gold under an encased fan leaves three gold nuggets, the coarse gold, and the fine washes away. Mercury catches the fine: two raw native gold and a mercury under a mixer give two gold amalgam, as the stamp mills' copper plates caught it.
pages.title: Panning and amalgam

pages.text: An amalgam heated in a basin gives off its mercury and leaves an electrum ingot, the mercury coming back about half the time.

Retorting amalgam in the open is how gold mining poisons people: the vapour is breathed. An amalgam in a basin hurts and poisons everyone within reach who has no diving helmet on a filled backtank, as small-scale miners from the Amazon to Indonesia are poisoned now.
pages.title: Mercury

pages.text: Cyanide replaced mercury in the 1890s, but it starts from hydrogen cyanide, made from methane and ammonia, which the pack does not have.

Electrum is gold and its silver. Miller's process blows chlorine through the melt and the silver leaves as its chloride: an electrum ingot and 250 mB of chlorine, superheated, give a gold ingot and a silver nugget. Or dissolve it in aqua regia, 500 mB heated, which leaves the silver as chloride and gives the same.
pages.title: Parting

pages.text: A furnace melts raw or crushed native gold to electrum, silver and all; only parting makes it gold.

Sources: Marsden and House, The Chemistry of Gold Extraction, 2nd ed. (SME, 2006); USGS, Mineral Commodity Summaries 2025, Gold; UNEP, Global Mercury Assessment 2018, artisanal and small-scale gold mining.
